content: The geologic time scale is a framework utilized by geologists and other scientists to describe the timing and relationships of events that have occurred throughout Earth's history. This time scale is based on the dates and nomenclature established by the International Commission on Stratigraphy and incorporates the standard color codes of the United States Geological Survey. Earth's geologic history, spanning approximately 4.6 billion years, is divided into various units based on significant events that occurred during each period. The divisions of the geologic time scale are often marked by major geological or paleontological events, such as mass extinction events. For instance, the boundary between the Cretaceous and Paleogene periods is defined by the Cretaceous–Tertiary extinction event, which led to the extinction of the dinosaurs and numerous marine species. Older periods, which predate the reliable fossil record, are defined by absolute ages rather than fossil evidence. The geologic time scale is hierarchically structured. The largest unit is the supereon, which is composed of eons. Eons are further divided into eras, which are subdivided into periods, epochs, and stages. Paleontologists also define faunal stages based on changes in fossil assemblages, and these stages are often incorporated into the geologic nomenclature. However, there are more recognized faunal stages than formally defined geologic time units. Geologists frequently use terms such as Upper/Late, Lower/Early, and Middle to describe parts of periods and other units, such as Upper Jurassic or Middle Cambrian. These terms are applied to rocks (e.g., Upper Jurassic sandstone) and time (e.g., Early Jurassic deposition). Formal subdivisions are capitalized (e.g., Early Jurassic), while informal ones are not (e.g., early Miocene). Because geologic units from the same time period can appear different and contain distinct fossils in different parts of the world, the same period has historically been given different names in various regions. For example, the Lower Cambrian is referred to as the Waucoban series in North America, subdivided into zones based on trilobites, while in East Asia and Siberia, it is divided into the Tommotian, Atdabanian, and Botomian stages. The International Commission on Stratigraphy works to reconcile these conflicting terminologies and establish universal horizons that can be applied globally. The principles underlying the geologic time scale were first proposed by Nicholas Steno in the late 17th century. Steno argued that rock layers (strata) are deposited in succession, with each layer representing a slice of time. He also formulated the principle of superposition, which states that any given stratum is older than the layers above it and younger than those below it. While these principles were straightforward, their application to real-world rock formations proved complex. During the 18th century, geologists recognized that sequences of strata were often eroded, distorted, tilted, or even inverted after deposition. They also realized that strata deposited simultaneously in different regions could have entirely different appearances and that the strata of any given area represented only a fraction of Earth's history. The first serious attempts to create a universal geologic time scale occurred in the late 18th century. Early efforts, such as those championed by Abraham Werner, divided Earth's rocks into four types: Primary, Secondary, Tertiary, and Quaternary. Each type was thought to correspond to a specific period in Earth's history. This framework allowed geologists to refer to a Tertiary Period as well as Tertiary Rocks. The terms Tertiary (now Paleocene–Pliocene) and Quaternary (now Pleistocene–Holocene) remained in use as names for geologic periods well into the 20th century. A major shift in geological thinking occurred with James Hutton's presentation of his Theory of the Earth in 1785. Hutton proposed that Earth's interior heat was the driving force behind the creation of new rock. He described a cycle in which land was eroded by air and water, deposited as layers in the sea, consolidated into stone by heat, and uplifted into new landmasses. This theory, known as Plutonism, contrasted with the flood-oriented Neptunist theories of the time. The identification of strata by their fossil content, pioneered by William Smith, Georges Cuvier, Jean d'Omalius d'Halloy, and Alexandre Brongniart in the early 19th century, allowed geologists to divide Earth's history more precisely. It also enabled the correlation of strata across national and even continental boundaries. If two strata contained the same fossils, it was likely that they were deposited at the same time. Detailed studies of European strata and fossils between 1820 and 1850 produced the sequence of geologic periods still used today. British geologists played a dominant role in this process, and many period names reflect this influence. For example, the Cambrian (from the Roman name for Wales), Ordovician, and Silurian (named after ancient Welsh tribes) were defined using stratigraphic sequences from Wales. The Devonian was named for the English county of Devon, and the Carboniferous was adapted from the Coal Measures, a term used by British geologists. The Permian was named after Perm, Russia, based on strata in that region defined by Scottish geologist Roderick Murchison. Some periods were defined by geologists from other countries. The Triassic was named in 1834 by German geologist Friedrich von Alberti for the three distinct layers (red beds, chalk, and black shales) found throughout Germany and Northwest Europe. The Jurassic was named by French geologist Alexandre Brongniart for the extensive marine limestone exposures in the Jura Mountains. The Cretaceous, named by Belgian geologist Jean d'Omalius d'Halloy in 1822, was defined using strata in the Paris Basin and named for the extensive beds of chalk (calcium carbonate deposited by marine invertebrate shells). British geologists also grouped periods into eras and subdivided the Tertiary and Quaternary periods into epochs. When William Smith and Sir Charles Lyell first recognized that rock strata represented successive time periods, time scales could only be estimated imprecisely due to the variability of rates of change used in estimation. While creationists proposed an Earth age of around six to seven thousand years based on the Bible, early geologists suggested millions of years for geologic periods, with some even proposing a virtually infinite age for Earth. Geologists and paleontologists constructed the geologic time scale based on the relative positions of different strata and fossils, estimating time scales by studying rates of weathering, erosion, sedimentation, and lithification. The discovery of radioactivity in 1896 and the development of radiometric dating in the early 20th century, pioneered by geologists like Arthur Holmes, allowed for more precise absolute dating of rocks. This resolved many debates about the ages of rock strata and Earth's age. In 1977, the Global Commission on Stratigraphy (now the International Commission on Stratigraphy) began efforts to define global reference points (Global Boundary Stratotype Sections and Points, or GSSPs) for geologic periods and faunal stages. A UML model for the structure of the time scale, relating it to the GSSPs, is also available.
